problem.text: The $y$-intercepts, $P$ and $Q$, of two perpendicular lines intersecting at the point $A(6,8)$ have a sum of zero. What is the area of $\triangle APQ$?

steps.title: Where to start: name the intercepts with one letter
steps.body: The clue is that the two $y$-intercepts add to zero. So they are opposites: $P = (0, p)$ and $Q = (0, -p)$ for some number $p$. Now there is only one unknown, and the word "perpendicular" should give us one equation for it.

your_turn.prompt: Why can we use a single letter $p$ for both intercepts?
your_turn.answer: If the $y$-coordinates add to $0$, one is the negative of the other; both points are on the $y$-axis, so their $x$-coordinates are $0$.

steps.title: Write the two slopes
steps.body: Line $AP$ goes through $A(6,8)$ and $P(0,p)$, and line $AQ$ goes through $A(6,8)$ and $Q(0,-p)$. Perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is $-1$.

your_turn.answer: Slope of $AP = \tfrac{8-p}{6}$ and slope of $AQ = \tfrac{8+p}{6}$ (rise over run from the $y$-axis to $A$).

steps.title: Solve for $p$
steps.body: Set the product of the slopes equal to $-1$: $$\frac{8-p}{6}\cdot\frac{8+p}{6} = -1,$$ so $64 - p^2 = -36$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: So $p = 10$: take $P = (0, 10)$ and $Q = (0, -10)$ ($p = -10$ just swaps the names). The right angle is at $A$, so the legs are $AP$ and $AQ$. By the distance formula, $AP = \sqrt{6^2 + 2^2} = 2\sqrt{10}$ and $AQ = \sqrt{6^2 + 18^2} = 6\sqrt{10}$. The area is $\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{10}\cdot 6\sqrt{10} = 60$. (Check: base $PQ = 20$ on the $y$-axis and height $6$, the distance from $A$ to the $y$-axis, also give $\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 20\cdot 6 = 60$.) The answer is **(D)**.
